title: Limit (mathematics)
description: Value approached by a mathematical object
wiki_lead:
In mathematics, a limit is the value that a function (or sequence) approaches as the argument (or index) approaches some value. Limits of functions are essential to calculus and mathematical analysis, and are used to define continuity, derivatives, and integrals.
The concept of a limit of a sequence is further generalized to the concept of a limit of a topological net, and is closely related to limit and direct limit in category theory.
The limit inferior and limit superior provide generalizations of the concept of a limit which are particularly relevant when the limit at a point may not exist.
The existence of a limit is called convergence.
wiki_excerpt:
In mathematics, a limit is the value that a function (or sequence) approaches as the argument (or index) approaches some value. Limits of functions are essential to calculus and mathematical analysis, and are used to define continuity, derivatives, and integrals.
The concept of a limit of a sequence is further generalized to the concept of a limit of a topological net, and is closely related to limit and direct limit in category theory.
The limit inferior and limit superior provide generalizations of the concept of a limit which are particularly relevant when the limit at a point may not exist.
The existence of a limit is called convergence.


Notation
In formulas, a limit of a function is usually written as
limx→cf(x)=L,
and is read as "the limit of f of x as x approaches c equals L". This means that the value of the function f can be made arbitrarily close to L, by choosing x sufficiently close to c. Alternatively, the fact that a function f approaches the limit L as x approaches c is sometimes denoted by a right arrow (→ or →), as in
f(x)→L as x→c,
or in
f(x)→x→cL,
which reads "f of x tends to L as x tends to c".


History
According to Hankel (1871), the modern concept of limit originates from Proposition X.1 of Euclid's Elements, which forms the basis of the Method of exhaustion found in Euclid and Archimedes: "Two unequal magnitudes being set out, if from the greater there is subtracted a magnitude greater than its half, and from that which is left a magnitude greater than its half, and if this process is repeated continually, then there will be left some magnitude less than the lesser magnitude set out."
Grégoire de Saint-Vincent gave the first definition of limit (terminus) of a geometric series in his work Opus Geometricum (1647): "The terminus of a progression is the end of the series, which none progression can reach, even not if she is continued in infinity, but which she can approach nearer than a given segment." 
In the Scholium to Principia in 1687, Isaac Newton had a clear definition of a limit, stating that "Those ultimate ratios ... are not actually ratios of ultimate quantities, but limits ... which they can approach so closely that their difference is less than any given quantity". Bruce Pourciau further argues that, in addition to Newton actually having a more sophisticated understanding of limits than he is generally credited with, he also provided the first epsilon argument.
The modern definition of a limit goes back to Bernard Bolzano who, in 1817, developed the basics of the epsilon-delta technique to define continuous functions. However, his work remained unknown to other mathematicians until thirty years after his death.
Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1821, followed by Karl Weierstrass, formalized the definition of the limit of a function which became known as the (ε, δ)-definition of limit.
The modern notation of placing the arrow below the limit symbol was invented by John Gaston Leathem in 1905 and popularized by G. H. Hardy's 1908 textbook A Course of Pure Mathematics.


Types of limits


In sequences


Real numbers
A sequence of real numbers a0,a1,… is said to converge to a limit L if the terms of the sequence give an arbitrarily good approximation of the number L, after discarding finitely many initial terms. An example is the sequence 0,0.3,0.33,0.333,0.3333, and so on. Each term in the sequence is an approximation to the rational number 1/3=0.333…. If an approximation is desired that lies within a given error ϵ, then all of the terms of the sequence except finitely many lie within the target error. For example, to get within ϵ=0.001 of 1/3, the approximations 0, 0.3, and 0.33 are outside the error window, but after discarding those three approximations, all of the remaining approximations are within the error range ϵ=0.001. The same approximation property holds for every positive error ϵ.
More precisely, a sequence {an}n∈ℕ of real numbers is said to be convergent if there exists an L∈ℝ such that for each positive real number ϵ, there exists a positive integer N (depending on ϵ) such that every term an with n>N is within distance ϵ of L. The number L is unique, when it exists. It is called the limit of the sequence {an}n∈ℕ, and this is written
limn→∞an=L.
The definition of the limit of a sequence can thus be summarized:

If such an L does not exist, {an}n∈ℕ is said to be divergent. 
A sequence is said to tend to infinity if all but finitely many terms exceed each given number. An example is the sequence 1,2,3,… of positive integers. This tends to infinity because, for any given bound M, every element of the sequence is greater than M after discarding the finite number that are not. Formally, {an}n∈ℕ tends to infinity if, given any real M, there exists a positive integer N such that an>M for every n>N. This is written as limn→∞an=∞. 
Similarly, the sequence is said to tend to negative infinity if all but finitely many terms are less than any given lower bound. This is written as limn→∞an=−∞.
In each case where limn→∞an=∞ or limn→∞an=−∞, the sequence is said to have an infinite limit. But it does not have a limit in the sense of being convergent to a real number, since ∞ and −∞ are not real numbers.


Metric space
The discussion of sequences above is for sequences of real numbers. The notion of limits can be defined for sequences valued in more abstract spaces, such as metric spaces. If M is a metric space with distance function d, and {an}n≥0 is a sequence in M, then the limit (when it exists) of the sequence is an element a∈M such that, given ε>0, there exists an N such that for each n>N, we have
d(a,an)<ε.
An equivalent statement is that an→a if the sequence of real numbers d(a,an)→0.

grok_lead: In mathematics, particularly within the fields of calculus and mathematical analysis, a limit is a foundational concept that quantifies the value toward which a function or sequence approaches as its input (or index) gets arbitrarily close to a specified point, even if the function is undefined or behaves differently exactly at that point. This idea captures the intuitive notion of "approaching" without requiring attainment, enabling the precise description of dynamic behaviors like rates of change and accumulations. Formally denoted as $ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L $, it signifies that the output values of $ f(x) $ can be made to lie within any small interval around $ L $ by restricting the input $ x $ to a sufficiently small punctured neighborhood of $ a $. The historical development of limits traces back to ancient Greece, where paradoxes posed by Zeno of Elea around 450 BCE challenged notions of infinity, motion, and divisibility, prompting early explorations of convergent processes. In the 3rd century BCE, Archimedes advanced these ideas through his method of exhaustion, which approximated areas and volumes by inscribing and circumscribing polygons around curves, effectively using limits to bound quantities without infinitesimals. The concept lay dormant until the 17th century, when Isaac Newton (circa 1665â1667) and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently invented calculus, employing intuitive infinitesimals to handle derivatives and integrals, though their approaches faced criticism for lacking rigor. Rigorous foundations emerged in the 19th century with Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who in 1821 defined limits in terms of successive approximations approaching a fixed value. This was refined by Karl Weierstrass in the 1850sâ1860s, who introduced the epsilon-delta formalism to eliminate ambiguities and establish analysis on a solid logical basis. The epsilon-delta definition provides the modern standard for limits of functions: $ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L $ if, for every $ \varepsilon > 0 $, there exists $ \delta > 0 $ such that whenever $ 0 < |x - a| < \delta $, it follows that $ |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon $. This quantifies "arbitrarily close" through tolerances $ \varepsilon $ and $ \delta $, ensuring the function's outputs stay within a desired band around $ L $ in a deleted neighborhood of $ a $, regardless of the function's value (or lack thereof) at $ a $ itself. Limits extend beyond functions to sequences, where $ \lim_{n \to \infty} a_n = L $ means the terms approach $ L $ as the index $ n $ grows indefinitely, and to infinite cases like $ \lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) $, describing asymptotic behavior. Limits are indispensable in mathematics, serving as the cornerstone for defining continuity (a function is continuous at $ a $ if $ \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a) $), derivatives (as limits of difference quotients), and integrals (as limits of Riemann sums). They enable the analysis of convergence in series, the study of differential equations, and applications across physics, engineering, and economics, such as modeling instantaneous rates or steady-state systems. Without limits, the precision of modern calculus and real analysis would be impossible, bridging intuitive approximations with rigorous proofs.
